extracted.subtask_description: Extract lessons and evaluative criteria for press releases and crisis communications from historical corporate and celebrity PR disasters; focuses on what to avoid, how to respond, and remedial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid careless/offhand remarks by executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Offhand remarks by leaders can trigger a publicity storm and destroy brand value (example: Gerald Ratner's 'because it's total crap').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive comments at informal events can be amplified by media; a single quote can cost millions, lead to job loss and force rebranding. Train spokespeople and leaders on message discipline; avoid derogatory descriptions of your own products or customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't deploy deceptive or fraudulent practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceptive corporate practices (e.g., VW's use of cheat software to give false exhaust readings) lead to massive reputational, legal and financial consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission of wrongdoing may require executive resignations, large civil and criminal penalties, multi-billion-dollar costs, and long-term brand damage. Transparency and compliance are essential; remedial actions can include fines, settlements, leadership changes and public remediation programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology wording must be sensitive and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Insensitive or self‑centred apologies (e.g., Tony Hayward's 'I'd like my life back') can worsen public anger and damage reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologies should acknowledge harm, show empathy, and outline concrete remedial steps. Poor phrasing can cost leaders their jobs and become emblematic of the mishandling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure product safety and manage recalls thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-safety failures and partially executed recalls (e.g., Samsung Galaxy Note 7 battery fires and ineffective replacements) can force complete withdrawal and cost billions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recalls must be comprehensive and verifiably effective; inadequate fixes can compound the crisis. Prioritise consumer safety, clear communication, and robust testing of replacement solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivializing or exploiting social issues in advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads that appear to trivialize protests or social movements (e.g., Pepsi ad with Kendall Jenner) are mocked as tasteless and insensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when referencing real-world social or political issues; tone-deaf creative can prompt rapid online backlash. If misstep occurs, promptly pull the ad, apologise sincerely, and avoid defensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be truthful in marketing claims; avoid misleading taglines
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing claims that are contradicted by practice (e.g., Tim Hortons' 'Always fresh' while serving frozen doughnuts) undermine trust and provoke legal and reputational consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure advertising claims are accurate and verifiable. Misleading taglines can trigger front‑page coverage, class actions, and long-term erosion of brand promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid evasive denials or obfuscation by spokespeople
rubrics_metrics.description: Evasive statements from company representatives (e.g., 'Until I confirm or deny anything, it simply doesn't exist.') exacerbate suspicion and outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train spokespeople to provide clear, honest, and timely information. Denial or obfuscation invites media scrutiny and legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't insult or stereotype your customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Derogatory characterisations of customers (e.g., Topman's director calling customers 'football hooligans') force apologies and damage customer relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that alienates core customer demographics; comments taken 'out of context' still require repair. Monitor media and trade interviews closely and prepare contextual messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise high risk of live-broadcast events
rubrics_metrics.description: Live broadcasts can produce sudden, uncontrollable PR crises (e.g., Janet Jackson's Super Bowl 'wardrobe malfunction'), leading to fines and lasting career impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for contingencies in live events, consider delay mechanisms and legal/regulatory exposure. Be prepared for rapid corporate response and downstream effects (both negative and unexpected beneficiaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider long-term ethical consequences of PR stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: PR stunts that manipulate social movements or behaviours (e.g., Bernays' 'Torches of Freedom' linking smoking to feminism) can have lasting societal harm and later backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethical implications and long-term impacts of campaigns. Short-term publicity can create long-term reputational risk and moral liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent incentive-driven misconduct and hold leadership accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressive sales targets and perverse incentives can drive employees to fraudulent acts (e.g., Wells Fargo fake accounts), resulting in mass firings, executive penalties and large settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ethical incentive structures, monitor for abuse, investigate complaints promptly, and ensure transparent accountability including restitution and, if necessary, leadership changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective actions must be effective, not merely symbolic
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions like recalls, ad pulls or slogan changes may be necessary but must actually address the root problem (VW changed slogan and paid penalties; Samsung's replacements still failed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine admissions/apologies with concrete remediation (product fixes, compensation, policy changes). Symbolic gestures without effective repair can prolong or deepen the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and external events influence public attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of a PR incident can be mitigated or amplified by timing and competing news (e.g., Pepsi controversy eclipsed by United Airlines incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that external events can shift focus; while timing can sometimes blunt backlash, organisations should not rely on luck. Use strategic timing for responses but prioritise prompt, appropriate action.
